section_1.title: Introduction: The Impossible Counting Problem
section_1.content: Introduce two blocks on a frictionless surface: a small block (mass m) and a large block (mass M). If M is a power of 100 (e.g., 100^n), the total number of elastic collisions between the blocks and a wall will exactly represent the first n+1 digits of Pi.
section_1.example: Visualize two colorful robots (a small red cube and a giant blue block) colliding on a frictionless track; the blue block is massive, and the red one bounces back and forth like a ping-pong ball.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
section_2.content: Briefly review the conservation of momentum (mv1 + Mv2 = constant) and kinetic energy in perfectly elastic collisions. Explain that these laws create a mathematical mapping between the physical system and a geometric rotation.
section_2.example: A 'collision diagram' showing a 2D space where the x and y axes represent the velocities of the two blocks. A collision is a reflection in this space.

section_3.title: The Geometry of Collisions: The Phase Space
section_3.content: Transform the collision problem into a geometric one. The state of the system traces a circular arc on a 2D plane. Each collision event corresponds to a reflection across a specific line determined by the mass ratio.
section_3.example: An animation showing the velocity vector of the blocks rotating around a circle; every time the vector hits a 'boundary line', it signifies a physical collision.

section_4.title: The Connection: Why Pi?
section_4.content: Explain that the total angle covered by the rotation is proportional to Pi. As the mass M becomes infinitely large, the boundary lines force the 'bouncing' to count out the value of Pi in base-10 increments.
section_4.example: A pie chart (pun intended) filling up piece by piece as the red block hits the blue block; each 'slice' added corresponds to a digit of 3.1415...

section_5.title: Conclusion: Computation through Nature
section_5.content: Summarize how a mechanical experiment acts as a digital computer. Emphasize that complex mathematical constants like Pi are embedded in the fundamental laws of motion.
section_5.example: Final screen showing: 1 collision = '3', 14 more = '1', 159 more = '4'... a 'Mechanical Pi Calculator'.

section_1.title: Introduction: The Impossible Counting Problem
section_1.content: Introduce two blocks on a frictionless surface: a small block (mass m) and a large block (mass M). If M is a power of 100 (e.g., 100^n), the total number of elastic collisions between the blocks and a wall will exactly represent the first n+1 digits of Pi.
section_1.example: Visualize two colorful robots (a small red cube and a giant blue block) colliding on a frictionless track; the blue block is massive, and the red one bounces back and forth like a ping-pong ball.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
section_2.content: Briefly review the conservation of momentum (mv1 + Mv2 = constant) and kinetic energy in perfectly elastic collisions. Explain that these laws create a mathematical mapping between the physical system and a geometric rotation.
section_2.example: A 'collision diagram' showing a 2D space where the x and y axes represent the velocities of the two blocks. A collision is a reflection in this space.

section_3.title: The Geometry of Collisions: The Phase Space
section_3.content: Transform the collision problem into a geometric one. The state of the system traces a circular arc on a 2D plane. Each collision event corresponds to a reflection across a specific line determined by the mass ratio.
section_3.example: An animation showing the velocity vector of the blocks rotating around a circle; every time the vector hits a 'boundary line', it signifies a physical collision.

section_4.title: The Connection: Why Pi?
section_4.content: Explain that the total angle covered by the rotation is proportional to Pi. As the mass M becomes infinitely large, the boundary lines force the 'bouncing' to count out the value of Pi in base-10 increments.
section_4.example: A pie chart (pun intended) filling up piece by piece as the red block hits the blue block; each 'slice' added corresponds to a digit of 3.1415...

section_5.title: Conclusion: Computation through Nature
section_5.content: Summarize how a mechanical experiment acts as a digital computer. Emphasize that complex mathematical constants like Pi are embedded in the fundamental laws of motion.
section_5.example: Final screen showing: 1 collision = '3', 14 more = '1', 159 more = '4'... a 'Mechanical Pi Calculator'.
